abstract: Temperature is molecular motion, but how living systems sense this is poorly understood. Many responses in plants integrate light and temperature signals, for example, via light receptors and the circadian clock. CONSTITUTIVE PHOTOMORPHOGENESIS 1 (COP1) regulates light signaling and is necessary for responding to temperature. We show that COP1 acts as a temperature-dependent switch, becoming activated by a warm temperature-induced conformational change. An intramolecular Val-Pro (VP) motif binds to the active site of COP1 at low temperatures, preventing substrate docking. At warmer temperatures, the VP motif becomes detached, enabling client proteins to bind and be degraded. This discovery explains how plants are able to obtain a precise readout of temperature within a given climate range. Altering the binding of the VP motif is sufficient to adjust the temperature range within which the plant responds. This helps us understand how plants are able to adapt to different climates.
title: COP1 is a temperature-responsive switch in Arabidopsis

abstract: As global energy markets grapple with a period of sustained political volatility, researchers are digging deep for solutions.
title: Can green technologies deliver energy security in an unstable world?

abstract: A framework for diagnosing obesity that was proposed in 2025 incorporates waist circumference and related measures and distinguishes clinical from preclinical obesity on the basis of obesity-induced organ dysfunction. In an international multi-cohort study of 844,108 adults, this framework outperformed conventional body-mass-index-based criteria in diagnosing obesity and stratifying mortality risk. A combination of body and organ-function metrics does better at classifying obesity than does body mass index.
title: Proposed approach for diagnosing obesity outperforms old method

abstract: Nuclear pores control molecular traffic into and out of the cell nucleus. Measurements in living cells, together with molecular-dynamics simulations, show that flexible protein chains that form the selectivity barriers of nuclear pores are highly mobile, and that a sugar modification and the carrier protein importin-β help to preserve this dynamic state. The motion of the nuclear pore protein NUP98 is regulated by a transport receptor and a sugar modification.
title: Proteins that form the nuclear pore barrier move like liquids

abstract: Forecasts of the effects that climate change will have on biodiversity typically rely on long-term climate averages while excluding extreme events. Projections that include severe drought predict that a majority of the 993 cactus species assessed will see large losses of suitable climatic area: more than 25% of species could lose at least 80% of it by 2100. Models that ignore extreme events might underestimate the dangers of climate change for this plant family.
title: Cacti are severely threatened by drought in a warming world

abstract: Ancient rocks in northern China reveal that by 3.95 billion years ago, surface-altered oceanic crust had been buried rapidly to depths greater than 50 kilometres and partly melted. This crust was derived from a mantle reservoir that had been left behind when the crust separated from the early mantle as early as 4.3 billion years ago. Zircon crystals found in some of Earth’s oldest rocks suggest that the source rock was once buried about 50 kilometres into the mantle.
title: Earth’s early history told by 3.9-billion-year-old rocks from northern China

abstract: Materials, at their essence, are networks defined by homogeneity: uniform bonds, fixed thicknesses, and discrete length scales. Mechanical metamaterials, while representing structurally more diverse microstructures, remain defined by the homogeneity of their unit cells, pore sizes, or repeating features. In contrast, as network science has revealed, real-world and biological systems -- from the Internet to the brain -- derive their function from broad, multiscale variability in connectivity and link length. Here, we introduce Scale-Rich (SR) metamaterials, a design framework that embeds network heterogeneity into mechanical metamaterials, achieving order-of-magnitude heterogeneity in ligament lengths, thicknesses, and connectivity. Governed by only two parameters, SR networks span orders of magnitude in structural features, overcoming prior constraints in metamaterial design. Translating these network models into physically realizable materials, we use simulations and experiments to show that SR metamaterials exhibit properties inaccessible to traditional single-scale systems, including highly tunable elastic anisotropy, delocalized nonlinear deformation with high energy absorption, and programmable acoustic wave control. This network-science-based paradigm establishes a minimal yet universal framework for engineering multifunctional materials whose mechanical and acoustic behavior emerge directly from scale diversity itself.
title: Scale-rich network-based metamaterials

abstract: Abstract Disruptions to leading-strand synthesis impair and stall replication forks because DNA synthesis by the leading-strand polymerase, Pol ε, is essential for optimal template unwinding by the replicative CMG (CDC45–MCM–GINS) helicase 1,2 . Failure to efficiently restart and/or protect stalled replication forks is a major source of genomic instability 3–6 . Stalled forks can be restarted by a variety of mechanisms, including repriming downstream of the impediment 4 . In human cells, the primase–polymerase PRIMPOL promotes fork progression during replication stress 7–10 , but how its activity is coordinated by the replisome is unresolved. Here, by reconstituting replication fork stalling and restart with purified human proteins, we show that the CMG helicase directs PRIMPOL for efficient replication fork restart. Unexpectedly, the interaction between PRIMPOL and replication protein A 9,11 is not critical for fork restart in this system. We show that PRIMPOL binds directly to CMG, and a cryo-electron microscopy structure illustrates how this targets PRIMPOL specifically for leading-strand priming to minimize the size of post-replicative gaps. Ablating the CMG–PRIMPOL interaction abolishes fork restart in vitro and PRIMPOL-dependent DNA damage tolerance in human cells. Our work establishes PRIMPOL as an integrated component of the human replisome dedicated to leading-strand priming.
title: Human replisomes direct a dedicated leading-strand primase for fork restart

abstract: Abstract In 2025, a Lancet Commission proposed distinguishing clinical obesity, defined by adiposity-related organ dysfunction, from preclinical obesity, defined by excess adiposity with preserved function, and recommended using anthropometric measures beyond body mass index (BMI) to confirm obesity status 1 . Here we report the comparative performance of this framework versus conventional BMI-based classification using prevalence, incidence and mortality data from 844,108 adults across four cohorts in China, the UK, the USA and Spain. Complementing BMI with waist circumference and waist-to-height ratio data showed that BMI alone overestimated obesity in 1.2–3.1% and underestimated it in 5.2–8.6% of participants across cohorts. The combined anthropometric definition increased overall obesity prevalence by 3.3–7.4% relative to BMI-based classification. Clinical obesity accounted for 22.7–31.3% of total obesity, with an overall population prevalence of 5.6–10.9%. A large proportion of individuals (between 77.4% and 91.3%) with preclinical obesity at baseline showed no progression to clinical obesity over 10 years. Increased mortality risk was associated with the combined anthropometric definition of obesity, but not with BMI-only obesity. Clinical obesity was associated with substantially higher all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 1.69, 95% confidence interval 1.64–1.73), whereas preclinical obesity conferred only modest risk (1.19, 1.14–1.24). These findings support the global adoption of the Lancet Commission diagnostic framework to improve obesity care and policy.
title: Validation of clinical and preclinical obesity across global cohorts

abstract: Abstract A new epoch for direct visualization of accretion dynamics near the event horizon of a black hole began when the Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration synthesized an Earth-sized aperture with millimetre radio interferometry and published the first reconstructed image 1–4 of a black hole shadow at the core of radio galaxy Messier 87 (M87). The image appeared as a ring-like structure, representing the gravitationally lensed and redshifted emission around the central supermassive black hole, M87*, located at the galactic nucleus. However, application of various data analysis and imaging heuristics resulted in divergent representations of M87* fine-scale features 3,5–7 , with some external analyses even challenging the fundamental ring-like morphology of the source 8,9 . Such difficulties arise as a consequence of the inherent sparsity of the very long baseline interferometry measurements, making interferometric image reconstruction an inadequately constrained problem. Moreover, the solution is sensitive to instrument calibration, post-processing algorithms and imaging hyperparameters. Here we apply an independent imaging algorithm that we have developed to the M87* dataset that is free from prescriptive morphological priors and founded on observables immune to instrument calibration errors. We reconstruct the black hole shadow image and unequivocally reproduce a ring-like morphology, with an angular diameter of 42.2 ± 1.5 μas corresponding to a black hole mass of 6.5 ± 0.5 billion solar masses assuming nominal scaling parameters, observed at an inclination angle of approximately 20° from the approaching jet.
title: Independent interferometric observable confirms black hole shadow in M87*

abstract: Abstract TDP-43 nuclear depletion is a defining pathological feature of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia that induces widespread cryptic splicing defects in hundreds of transcripts 1–8 . Despite this, whether TDP-43 loss affects synaptic function has remained unclear. Here we show that TDP-43 loss induces a predegenerative state in which neurons remain structurally intact but suffer a substantial breakdown in synaptic communication. Genetic correction of a single cryptic splicing event in UNC13A was sufficient to rescue these deficits. We developed splice-switching antisense oligonucleotides that correct UNC13A cryptic splicing in human cortical and spinal motor neurons and in a humanized mouse model. In human neurons this intervention restored spontaneous and evoked synaptic vesicle release, release probability at individual synapses and wider network synchrony. Together, this establishes UNC13A splice correction as a mechanistically defined and genetically validated therapeutic strategy relevant to roughly 97% of patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and roughly 50% of patients with frontotemporal dementia with TDP-43 pathology.
title: UNC13A splice correction rescues synaptic dysfunction induced by TDP-43 loss

abstract: Abstract The nuclear pore complex (NPC) regulates molecular traffic between nucleus and cytoplasm 1,2 . Its permeability barrier is formed by intrinsically disordered phenylalanine-glycine-rich nucleoporins (FG-NUPs), whose physical state has long been debated 3–13 . Deciphering how FG-NUPs behave inside living cells is crucial for understanding how NPCs achieve both selective and rapid transport. By combining site-specific labelling with time-resolved fluorescence anisotropy, here we show that FG domains exhibit nanosecond-scale, liquid-like segmental motion in live cells, whereas reconstituted FG condensates undergo a liquid-to-solid transition in vitro. Experiments and molecular-dynamics simulations further show that importin-β, a principal nuclear transport receptor, and O-linked β- N -acetylglucosamine, a key post-translational modification of FG-NUPs, together stabilize the dynamic FG network. Finely balanced FG–FG and FG–importin-β interactions maintain FG-NUP liquidity and generate a radial organization in which importin-β is enriched near the NPC periphery and extended FG domains remain in the central channel, forming the transport barrier. This organization explains recent MINFLUX observations 14 of rim-biased transport trajectories and is supported here by direct MINFLUX imaging of importin-β in mammalian cells. Together, our results reconcile conflicting models of FG-NUP organization 4,5,7,9,15 and establish a framework for understanding how cellular context tunes intrinsically disordered proteins in health and disease.
title: Glycosylation and importins liquefy the FG barrier in live nuclear pores

abstract: Abstract Transcriptional addiction to the androgen receptor (AR) underlies metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer 1 , in which AR maintains oncogenic programs through domain-specific interactions with the acetyltransferases p300 and CBP (collectively p300/CBP) 2 . Here we describe a novel therapeutic modality, domain-alteration chimeras (DALTACs), that rewire endogenous protein complexes by enforcing non-native domain–domain interactions. Our first-in-class AR–p300/CBP DALTAC-1 induces synthetic proximity between the ligand-binding domain of AR and the bromodomain of p300/CBP, misconfiguring their native interface and locking the complex in a non-productive state. DALTAC-1 triggers a ‘super-inhibitory’ effect, suppressing AR-driven transcription and proliferation more potently than combined AR and p300/CBP inhibition. Mechanistically, DALTAC-1 reprograms p300/CBP substrate engagement, abolishing the histone mark H2B N-terminal acetylation and inducing neomorphic acetylation of AR and coactivators, ultimately collapsing the AR neo-enhanceosome. Chromatin profiling revealed redistribution of AR and p300/CBP towards palindromic androgen response elements, accompanied by disruption of cofactor and transcriptional machinery recruitment at oncogenic AR and ERG neo-enhancers. DALTAC-1 exhibits exquisite lineage selectivity, displaying potent activity in AR–p300/CBP dual-dependent cells and sparing AR-negative cells. In multiple in vivo models, DALTAC-1 induces deep and durable tumour regressions. Together, these findings establish DALTACs as a broadly applicable strategy to rewire disease-defining complexes through domain-topology alteration, expanding induced-proximity therapies, and the precise lineage selectivity of DALTAC-1 supports its translational potential in AR-driven prostate cancer.
title: Domain-alteration chimeras rewire oncogenic complexes in prostate cancer

abstract: Abstract Somatic evolution in ageing tissues underlies many cancers 1,2 . However, our quantitative understanding of the rules governing this pre-cancerous evolution remains incomplete. Here we exploit a unique collection of serial blood samples 3 , collected annually for up to a decade and beginning as early as 15 years before diagnosis of acute myeloid leukaemia, to provide a quantitative description of pre-cancerous evolutionary dynamics. Using deep duplex sequencing and evolutionary theory, we quantify the acquisition ages and fitness effects of the key driver events in acute myeloid leukaemia development. The first driver mutations are typically acquired in the first few decades of life, when the blood remains highly polyclonal. These early slow-growing clones subsequently acquire multiple further driver mutations that confer selective advantages up to 100-fold larger than the early drivers. These faster-growing clones harbouring multiple driver mutations can cause complete somatic sweeps of the blood decades before diagnosis, a feature strongly associated with future acute myeloid leukaemia. Our data show that the clonal dynamics of blood are consistent with a set of remarkably simple evolutionary rules that strike a balance between chance and determinism.
title: Evolutionary dynamics in the years preceding acute myeloid leukaemia

abstract: Abstract Aggressive scaling in silicon electronics—although essential for improving power, performance, area and cost—faces increasing challenges in further reducing power consumption due to electrostatic and leakage constraints 1,2 . Achieving efficient operation at low supply voltages therefore requires new materials and gate-stack engineering strategies. Two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors offer intrinsic advantages because their atomic thickness affords excellent gate control, and their sizable bandgaps suppress off-state current. However, a major obstacle is the imperfect interface between 2D channels and gate dielectrics, which degrades subthreshold swing, hysteresis and bias-temperature instability 3 . Here we demonstrate that a wafer-scale, transferable, single-crystal anatase titanium dioxide dielectric can be van der Waals integrated with 2D transition metal dichalcogenides. The obtained pristine 2D-dielectric interface enables subthreshold swing close to the thermal limit, record-low hysteresis and well-matched transfer characteristics for both n- and p-type enhancement-mode field-effect transistors. Building on this, we demonstrate complementary field-effect transistors, whose inverters achieve high voltage gain and large noise margins with subpicowatt static power consumption. These results highlight the promise of 2D semiconductors for ultra-low-power operation.
title: Low-power 2D CFETs using single-crystal high-κ dielectrics

abstract: Abstract The global transition towards sustainable energy systems has identified tidal power as a uniquely predictable and substantial renewable energy resource 1 . However, the highly unsteady sea environment subjects turbines to severe hydrodynamic loads, greatly increasing capital and maintenance costs 2,3 . Large-scale state-of-the-art turbines at present rely on complex, expensive active pitch systems to mitigate these fluctuations. Here we present a reliable, passive alternative: flexible rubber blades featuring chordwise trailing-edge deformation. We experimentally demonstrate that these flexible blades achieve an equivalent total energy yield over simulated tidal cycles compared with rigid blades with active pitch control, while mitigating high-frequency fatigue-inducing load fluctuations by up to one-third. This passive load regulation arises from aeroelastic deformation that flattens blade camber under load, enabling structural robustness without added mechanical complexity. These findings suggest that chordwise-flexible blades can enhance the durability and performance of tidal turbines, offering a promising pathway towards more reliable and cost-effective tidal energy generation.
title: Flexible rubber blades for tidal turbines

abstract: Abstract The scarcity of terrestrial rocks older than 3.9 billion years (Ga) has hindered our understanding of Earth’s early evolution, fueling persistent debates on how and when the first continental crust formed and plate tectonics started. Currently, the only unequivocally documented >3.9 Ga rocks are from the Acasta Gneiss Complex, Canada 1–3. Here we report a newly discovered 3.95 Ga trondhjemitic gneiss from eastern Hebei, North China Craton, where 3.95 Ga magmatic zircon records elevated δ18O values (average +6.77 ± 0.23‰) and positive εHf(t) (weighted mean +1.45 ± 0.27), indicating a low-temperature altered basaltic source that originated from a Hadean depleted mantle. In contrast to the low-pressure origin inferred for the ca. 4.0 Ga Acasta rocks 2, the 3.95 Ga trondhjemitic gneiss reported here exhibits geochemical signatures attributed to a high-pressure origin 4. Thermodynamic and trace element modelling demonstrates that its parental magma formed via low degree (8–16%) melting of basaltic crust at >1.6 GPa and 740–820 ℃, suggesting rapid burial of (near-)surface‑altered oceanic crust to mantle depths along a cool thermal gradient. We propose that this rapid burial was most likely achieved through a transient subduction event.
title: Hadean mantle depletion and 3.95-Gyr subduction implied by North China rocks

abstract: Abstract Accessing reversible four-electron iodine redox chemistry in aqueous metal–iodine batteries offers a promising route towards high-energy aqueous energy storage, but has conventionally relied on highly concentrated, corrosive halogen-containing electrolytes to stabilize reactive hypervalent iodine cations through interhalogen complexation 1–9 . Here we show a kosmotropic anion–polar anion–nucleophilic species (Nuc) electrolyte framework that harnesses anionic chemistry to coordinate the interfacial microenvironment and molecular interactions, enabling reversible four-electron iodine conversion in halogen-free aqueous electrolytes. Polar anions establish a water-deficient, anion-enriched interfacial microenvironment, whereas kosmotropic anions regulate water–Nuc interactions to increase the availability of Nuc for stabilizing hypervalent iodine cations through Nuc–I + –Nuc halogen bonds. This electrolyte framework is validated across diverse Nuc and in both aqueous Zn–I 2 and Al–I 2 batteries. Moving beyond conventional interhalogen stabilization, these findings establish a distinct electrolyte chemistry framework and represent a mechanistic shift for reversible multi-electron iodine chemistry in aqueous environments.
title: Non-halogen aqueous electrolytes for four-electron iodine conversion

abstract: Abstract Plastic pollution is a defining feature of the Anthropocene 1 , and microplastics are dispersed by air and water into even remote terrestrial habitats 2–7 , yet the ecological and landscape-level processes that shape microplastic accumulation in terrestrial ecosystems remain poorly understood. Human land-use change is rapidly transforming landscapes worldwide, but the influence of this expanding human footprint on the microplastic burdens in wildlife remains largely unknown. This knowledge gap is particularly pressing in regions that are facing escalating environmental pressures, such as Brazil. Here we pair in vivo microplastic measurements with high-resolution tracking data from lowland tapirs and giant anteaters across Brazil and show that the microplastic burdens carried by free-ranging mammals increase with both the magnitude of their human footprint exposure and their proximity to development and waste management infrastructure. Microplastics were also detected in the blood of individuals occupying seemingly pristine habitats far from development, suggesting that direct exposure to human-modified landscapes is unlikely to be the sole driver of systemic microplastic burdens. In a period of accelerating global land-use change, these findings reveal how individual habitat use and anthropogenic land-use change interact to shape wildlife exposure to microplastics and suggest that managing animals’ proximity to development and waste management infrastructure may reduce the microplastic burdens carried by terrestrial wildlife.
authors: Marcia de Almeida Monteiro Melo Ferraz
title: Human land use drives microplastic abundance in terrestrial wildlife

abstract: Abstract Brown adipocytes (BAs) are thermogenic cells that regulate energy homeostasis, and age-related declines in thermogenesis contribute to cold sensitivity 1–5 . We previously identified a BA subpopulation with low UCP1 expression (hereafter, BA-L cells) that coexists with the classical, high-UCP1-expressing BAs (hereafter, BA-H cells) 6 . Here we show that IL-1β secreted by neutrophils and macrophages stabilizes nearby BAs in the BA-L state. Specifically, IL-1β stabilizes hexose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (H6PD) protein from degradation to ensure the generation of active glucocorticoids, which activate the glucocorticoid receptor (GR, encoded by Nr3c1 ) and increase the expression of its target gene, regulator of G-protein signalling 2 ( Rgs2 ), thereby suppressing UCP1 expression. Cold exposure reduces IL-1β levels, depending on sympathetic innervation, leading to H6PD degradation and the conversion of BA-L cells to BA-H cells, thereby enhancing UCP1-dependent thermogenesis. Rising environmental temperatures trigger the opposite events. BA-specific inducible deletion of Nr3c1 during cold exposure locks these cells in the BA-H state, leading to persistent thermogenesis and increased energy expenditure days after the mice return to room temperature. Notably, IL-1β is elevated in aged brown adipose tissue, resulting in a locked low BA-H/BA-L ratio and cold intolerance. Suppressing GR in aged mice restores the BA-H/BA-L ratio, resumes thermogenesis and increases energy expenditure. Our findings reveal a spatiotemporal neuronal–immune regulation of BA heterogeneity that governs thermogenesis and offers a fundamental understanding of the mechanisms underlying increased cold sensitivity in older individuals.
title: Bistable regulation of adipocyte heterogeneity governs thermogenesis

abstract: Microbial communities often exhibit apparently complex dynamics driven by myriad interactions among community members and with their environments. Yet, practical modeling and control are often based on a limited number of observables, raising fundamental questions: are these observed dynamics low-dimensional? If so, how does the low dimensionality enable predictions with limited information? Here, we report an emergent simplicity that the temporal dynamics of observable microbial populations can be captured by low-dimensional representations. Using variational autoencoders, we define a critical latent dimension ( E c ) that operationally quantifies the smallest latent dimension required for high-fidelity reconstruction of observable microbial dynamics under a specified criterion. Despite the complexity of unobserved background dynamics, we find E c to be drastically lower than the community’s apparent degrees of freedom. E c scales linearly with the number of observables, providing an empirical principle for determining representation complexity. This principle holds across simulations of pairwise interacting communities, consumer–resource dynamics, spatially distributed microbial patches, and plasmid transfer, experiments with engineered and environment-derived communities, and human microbiomes. Our findings establish a scaling law for microbial community dynamics and demonstrate that low-dimensional representations of observable dynamics retain information useful for selected prediction tasks without direct measurement of the complete community.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Linear scaling reveals low-dimensional structure in observable microbial dynamics

abstract: Dysregulated MYC provokes profound changes in cancer gene expression. Although usually considered an E-box-dependent transcription activator, an alternate model is that MYC is a universal amplifier of transcription. Although MYC participates in pause release, its full role in the transcription cycle remains poorly illuminated. MYC also stimulates topoisomerases to resolve DNA topological issues complicating its transactions; how this stimulation is coordinated with its transcriptional role has not been examined. We have developed a system that discriminates between MYC-driven activation versus amplification in any cell. This system enables the interrogation of genes, cofactors, and compounds that execute or modulate MYC activity. Using a combination of biochemical and cellular assays, we reveal dynamic interplay between MYC-driven transcription amplification and DNA supercoiling. Because the early stages of transcription are sensitive to DNA supercoiling, Reducing TOP1 activity 1 either through genetic knockdown or low-dose inhibition, potentiates transcription amplification by MYC. By increasing promoter melting and RNA polymerase loading, negative supercoiling provides the early transcription complexes upon which MYC acts to increase output.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Dynamic supercoiling sponsors transcription amplification by MYC

abstract: Natural ligaments are soft connective tissues that provide high stretchability for dexterous flexibility but switch to high stiffness to protect the musculoskeletal system from excessive deformation. These two functions cannot be independently tuned in conventional engineering materials with linear or hyperelasticity. Biological materials achieve this tailored behavior through a highly nonlinear tensile response characterized by a J-shaped curve, featuring an extended “toe region” of low force up to intermediate strains followed by an inflection, called the “heel region” which marks the onset of nonlinear stiffening. Here, we aim to study the characteristics of J-curves to establish principles for their use in robotic mechanisms. We define and measure the J-curve features responsible for protectiveness and mobility, describe the effective stiffness and the level of nonlinearity as a function of pre-stretch, and elucidate how the J-curve decouples flexibility from damage protection. Experimental measurements reveal the performance advantages of twisted and coiled elastomeric J-curve materials in engineered antagonistic arrangements and highlight their unique design space compared with linear elastic systems. Furthermore, we present a conceptual analysis of exploiting J-curve materials in energy-efficient running as an outlook toward their use in bioinspired robots.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Principles of use of tensile J-curve materials in antagonistic arrangements

abstract: Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) is a chronic neurodegenerative disorder, and elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) represents its only modifiable risk factor. We modeled increased IOP by treating three primary human trabecular meshwork cell strains with dexamethasone and generated a high-resolution map of promoter-centered chromatin contacts and regulatory modules. We identify dynamic changes in chromatin compartments and looping, cis-regulatory elements, and transcription factor hubs corresponding to altered expression profile. By integrating Genomewide association studies associated variants with dexamethasone induced chromatin landscape, we ascertain 29 target genes linked to 23 lead IOP variants and 57 genes for 46 POAG variants, with 19 shared between the two. Pathway analysis of 67 IOP- and POAG-associated genes reveals enrichment in vesicle transport, TLR, MAPK, and hippo-YAP signaling pathways. We also uncover transcriptional regulatory role of 103 noncoding lead variants. Our studies provide a mechanistic framework of genetic complexity accompanying steroid-induced IOP and related POAG pathology.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Chromatin dynamics secondary to dexamethasone exposure identifies 67 genes linked to elevated IOP and primary open-angle glaucoma

abstract: Excessive alcohol consumption frequently co-occurs with anxiety and depression in alcohol use disorder (AUD), yet the specific neural circuits and molecular mechanisms coordinating these comorbid conditions remain poorly defined. The medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), particularly its prelimbic (PL) and infralimbic (IL) subregions, projects to key reward and emotion centers like the nucleus accumbens (Nac) and basolateral amygdala (BLA), but the functional heterogeneity of these projections is unclear. Using chemogenetics, retrograde tracing, electrophysiology, spatial proteomics, and cell-type-specific gene editing in mice subjected to a 4-wk intermittent access to alcohol (IAA) paradigm, we selectively manipulated glutamatergic projections from the PL and IL to the Nac core, Nac shell, and BLA and assessed alcohol intake, anxiety-like, and depression-like behaviors. Chemogenetic activation of PL-Nac core projections reduced short-term alcohol intake, anxiety-, and depression-like behaviors, while IL-BLA activation decreased alcohol consumption and anxiety-like behaviors only. Retrograde tracing revealed mirror-image anatomical segregation of projection-defined neuronal subpopulations within PL/IL linking spatial organization to functional divergence. IAA induced pathway-specific synaptic adaptations. Spatial proteomics nominated protein phosphatase 1 regulatory subunit 1B (PPP1R1B) as a candidate molecule in PL-Nac core neurons. Independent immunostaining confirmed PPP1R1B downregulation, and circuit-specific knockout recapitulated alcohol-related and affective phenotypes, whereas overexpression reversed them. In IL-BLA neurons, PPP1R1B manipulation modulated alcohol intake and anxiety, but not depression. These findings define a subregion- and projection-specific organizational logic in the mPFC for differentially regulating alcohol consumption and emotional comorbidity, with PPP1R1B as a key molecular determinant. This provides a neural pathway–molecule framework for targeted intervention in AUD.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: PPP1R1B differentially modulates alcohol intake and emotional comorbidity through distinct prefrontal circuits

abstract: White matter free water (FW-WM), quantified using diffusion MRI, reflects extracellular water content and microstructural alterations within water matter, but its genetic architecture and clinical relevance remain largely uncharted. We conducted a multi-omics study integrating 42,039 individuals from the UK Biobank and Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative cohorts to characterize tract-specific FW-WM across genetic, phenotypic, and proteomic dimensions. Genome-wide association analyses identified 27 independent loci and prioritized 88 genes, which were enriched in the genomic functional elements of vascular endothelial cells, pericytes, and astrocytes. Notably, 20 loci (74%) were novel compared to conventional white matter metrics. Both genetic predisposition to higher FW-WM and imaging-derived FW-WM were associated with a spectrum of neurological disorders. Specifically, imaging-derived FW-WM showed strong associations with stroke (OR = 3.14) and dementia (OR = 4.15), while higher baseline FW-WM predicted progression from MCI to AD (HR = 2.58). Bidirectional Mendelian randomization analyses further supported genetically predicted associations between hypertension and FW-WM, which were together associated with increased risks of stroke and cognitive impairment. Integrative proteomic analyses further nominated PEAR1 and ANGL3 as candidate proteins potentially linking hypertension-related vascular processes to FW-WM variation. Together, these findings provide a multi-omics characterization of FW-WM that connects genetic susceptibility, vascular factors, and neurological outcomes, supporting FW-WM as a tract-specific imaging phenotype with potential utility for neurological risk stratification.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Multi-omics characterization of white matter free water reveals genetic and vascular determinants of neurological disorders

abstract: The process of speciation, through which two reproductively isolated species emerge from an ancestral population, is often gradual, including a period during which gene flow still occurs, and hence speciation remains reversible. However, if isolation persists, the progressive accumulation of genetic incompatibilities ultimately locks the speciation process, reaching the point where hybrid offspring are inviable or sterile. In plants and animals, the establishment of species barriers is quite rapid: Beyond a net genetic divergence of 0.02 substitutions per synonymous site, interspecific introgressions become extremely rare. Here we report that in ciliates, species barriers can be broken despite huge genetic divergence. We show that the genome of Paramecium sonneborni contains hundreds of DNA segments that were acquired by recurrent horizontal transfers from multiple very distant lineages (synonymous divergence ~1 substitution/site). These segments approach the size of full-length chromosomes, which indicates that they were introgressed by interspecific mating. These data show that in the ancestry of P. sonneborni , hybridization events with highly divergent species occurred repeatedly and led to viable and fertile offspring. We propose that this unexpected promiscuous sexual behavior is made possible by the fact that paramecia separate somatic and germline functions in two types of nuclei: The elimination of non-self-DNA fragments during the development of the somatic genome allows individuals of a species to remain phenotypically the same, despite recurrent genetic flow from distant species into their germline.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Recurrent hybridization between highly divergent paramecium species

abstract: In nature, plants perceive and respond to complex vegetative environments through the phytochrome (phy) photoreceptor-signaling system. The Canopy Adaptation Strategy, elicited by phyA, together with the Shade Avoidance Syndrome, regulated by phyB, enables plants to adapt to diverse forms of vegetation shade. The phyA High Irradiance Response mode, which involves photocycle-coupled nuclear shuttling, is essential for sensing sustained far-red-rich conditions typical of canopy or occlusive shade. Our research identifies PHYTOCHROME INTERACTING FACTOR 7 (PIF7) as a key regulator of phyA function. We show that PIF7 overexpression (PIF7ox) effectively suppresses phyA action. Under persistent shade, PIF7 and phyA both accumulate and associate within nuclear photobodies, with this interaction mediated by the C-terminal domain of PIF7 and the PAS-PAS domain of phyA. PIF7 also interacts with FAR-RED ELONGATED HYPOCOTYL 1 (FHY1) and FHY1-LIKE transport facilitators, thereby interfering with phyA cytosolic-nuclear shuttling. This coordinated molecular targeting by PIF7 constitutes an effective strategy for modulating phyA function under persistent shade conditions.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: PHYTOCHROME INTERACTING FACTOR 7 moderates the activity of phytochrome A in persistent canopy shade conditions

abstract: Extracellular signal-regulated kinases (ERKs) have essential roles in development and are implicated in numerous diseases. ERKs are activated by phosphorylation and are regulated by dephosphorylation. To study the ERK phosphatases, we adapted a method to monitor ERK activity in live, unfixed preparations that accommodates the highly dynamic temporal and spatial features of ERK activation. We evaluated 140 human phosphatases using an in vivo reporter (ERK-SPARK) for high-throughput screening in human cells, and we used an in vivo Drosophila model for functional validation of their phosphatase homologs. We found that EYA family phosphatases are critical regulators of ERK signaling both in Drosophila and in mammalian cells and found that inhibition of human EYA4, a homolog of Drosophila Eyes Absent phosphatase, enhances migration of ERK-responsive tumor cells. These findings have important implications for the development of therapeutics.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Phosphatases regulating ERK activation and ERK-dependent cell migration

abstract: The electron transport chain is a signaling hub for hydrogen sulfide (H 2 S) that serves both as a respiratory substrate and an inhibitor. While acute sulfide toxicity is well characterized, cellular adaptations to chronic H 2 S, particularly microbially-derived sulfide exposure in colon, is poorly understood. We report that chronic, low-level H 2 S exposure (4 to 20 µM) drives robust carbon sequestration in lipid droplets (LD) across several human cell lines, driven by a coordinated remodeling of redox and nucleotide metabolism. Specifically, H 2 S-induced reductive shifts in nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and coenzyme Q (CoQ) pools are accompanied by glycerol-3-phosphate accumulation and cytidine triphosphate (CTP) depletion. Lipidomic analysis reveals increased neutral lipid synthesis and triacylglyceride accumulation concomitant with decreased CTP-dependent synthesis of membrane phospholipids. Mitochondrial expression of a water-generating NADH oxidase attenuates LD accumulation and spatially confines the origin of H 2 S-induced reductive stress signaling to this compartment. Interestingly, LD abundance increases even after H 2 S withdrawal, continuing over 48 h, during which time the reductively-shifted NAD and CoQ pools slowly reoxidize. Inhibition of fatty acid synthesis during sulfide exposure impairs cellular recovery of respiration. These findings establish an active role for LDs in stress response and reveal that lipid biogenesis is a strategy for countering H 2 S-induced redox imbalance. The sulfide–LD–redox axis uncovered in this study has implications for understanding how gut-derived H 2 S, shaped by diet and microbiome, can influence metabolic health.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Lipid droplets buffer hydrogen sulfide–induced redox imbalance

abstract: Efficiently locating rare targets requires balancing the exploration of novel space with the exploitation of local vicinities. While this tradeoff is well documented in simplified environments, its behavior in realistic three-dimensional environments remains unclear. Here, we analyze intermittent Lévy walks in three dimensions and show that search efficiency becomes strongly dependent on target geometry, with volume, surface area, and elongation governing performance across the Lévy spectrum. Against this geometric complexity, the Cauchy walk ( μ = 2 ) emerges as a robust, near-optimal solution across a wide range of target geometries. Specifically, we prove that for convex targets of surface area Δ in a domain of volume n , the optimal expected detection time scales as n / Δ , and that the Cauchy walk achieves this scaling up to polylogarithmic factors, while other Lévy strategies are suboptimal in different geometric regimes. Our findings provide a theoretical framework for biological movement patterns, including marine predator foraging and immune surveillance, and inform the design of efficient search algorithms for engineered systems such as autonomous nanoscale explorers.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Intermittent Cauchy walks enable optimal 3D search across target shapes and sizes

abstract: Ecosystems are complex adaptive systems in which local interactions among individuals shape macroscopic phenomena such as pattern formation, multistability, and critical transitions. However, how such bottom-up interactions govern emergent behaviors and system-level complexity remains a central challenge in ecology. Phase transition theory, a classic paradigm in physics, links local interaction rules to emergent changes in macroscopic system states, offering a formal language for understanding cross-scale dynamics. Here we unite this theory with empirical evidence from dryland shrub–grass ecosystems and show that these systems exhibit three hallmarks of phase transitions. First, abrupt shifts separate different phases of deserts, shrublands, and grasslands. Second, shrublands and grasslands self-organize into Turing-like phase patterns, contrasting with homogeneous deserts. Third, special phenomena emerge near-transition threshold, including patch enlargement and abrupt decline at desert–vegetation interface, and fairy circles within the shrub–grass transition zone. Using a cellular automaton model built on a fundamental trade-off between extensive and intensive resource foraging strategies (EI trade-off), we show how kernels encoding local trade-offs integrate these seemingly disparate phenomena within a unified phase transition framework. Moreover, this EI trade-off was empirically validated through analyses of plant functional traits and spatial patterns of plant patches. These findings illustrate that dryland ecosystem dynamics reflect universal self-organization principles. Our work establishes phase-transition theory as a powerful framework for understanding, predicting, and managing complexity in dryland ecosystems, which advances the integration of complexity science with ecology, offering a pathway toward bottom-up ecosystem understanding.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Phase transition in a dryland shrub–grass ecosystem: Emergence through local trade-offs

abstract: Endometriosis is a steroid-dependent gynecologic disease characterized by progesterone (P4) resistance, subfertility/infertility, and pelvic pain; however, the molecular mechanisms underlying impaired P4 responsiveness in endometriosis tissue are not fully understood. RE1 silencing transcription factor (REST), a transcriptional regulator implicated in steroid hormone signaling, has emerged as a potential mediator of P4 responsiveness. Here, we investigated the role of REST in endometriosis using human tissues and a uterine-specific Rest conditional knockout mouse model. Immunohistochemical analysis of eutopic endometrium and ectopic lesions from patients with endometriosis revealed significantly reduced nuclear REST expression compared with control endometrium, suggesting loss of functional REST in disease. To assess the physiological consequences of REST deficiency, uterine-specific Rest knockout (Rest d/d ) mice were generated. Rest d/d females exhibited progressive subfertility and hyperestrogenic uterine tissue characteristics that displayed a blunted responsiveness to P4 treatment. Loss of Rest selectively altered expression of P4-responsive genes associated with endometriosis pathology, despite preserved P4 receptor expression. Following induction of experimental endometriosis, female mice that developed endometriotic-like lesions using Rest-deficient donor tissue developed significantly larger lesions that were less responsive to P4 treatment compared to lesions induced using control tissue. Mechanical sensitivity was modestly increased in mice receiving Rest-deficient tissue, whereas vaginal hyperalgesia was unaffected. These findings identify loss of nuclear REST as a feature of endometriosis and support a role of REST in subfertility, lesion progression, and blunted response to P4. REST may represent a molecular contributor to altered P4 responsiveness and a potential therapeutic target in endometriosis.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: RE1 silencing transcription factor is reduced in endometriosis, and uterine deletion in mice alters progesterone responsiveness

abstract: Methylation is a fundamental post-translational modification best understood as regulating chromatin structure and gene expression, yet there is emerging evidence that methylation also shapes cytoskeletal organization, regulating key processes such as mitosis and cell migration. Proteomic studies have revealed cytoskeletal protein methylation is widespread, however little is known about the enzymes responsible for these modifications, or their evolutionary relationship to other, better known substrates for methylation, such as chromatin. To address this question, we applied phylogenetic profiling across the complete repertoire of human methyltransferases to identify conserved functional relationships extending beyond chromatin. Unbiased clustering revealed extensive coevolution between methyltransferases and many components of the cytoskeleton, uncovering a previously unrecognized evolutionary network linking canonical chromatin regulatory enzymes to cellular structural systems. Evolutionary Trace analysis of the H3K36 methyltransferase family recovered known catalytic and regulatory domains while identifying additional evolutionarily constrained residues, suggesting previously unappreciated functional interfaces. Comparative analyses further distinguished deeply conserved methyltransferase–cytoskeletal relationships from those that emerged later during eukaryotic evolution, indicating that cytoskeletal methylation comprises both ancient and lineage-expanded regulatory programs. Leveraging these evolutionary signatures, we identified and experimentally validated a previously unrecognized association between the methyltransferase NSD3 and α-tubulin. Together, these findings reveal that methyltransferases traditionally viewed as chromatin regulators participate in an evolutionarily conserved network that coordinates nuclear and cytoskeletal functions. More broadly, they establish phylogenetic profiling as a powerful approach for discovering noncanonical activities of chromatin-associated enzymes and suggest that regulation of chromatin organization and cellular architecture evolved as interconnected processes.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Phylogenetic profiling reveals evolutionary coupling between methyltransferases and the cytoskeleton

abstract: Gout flare is driven by hyperuricemia (HUA) and inflammatory responses to monosodium urate (MSU) crystals, yet single time-point serum uric acid (UA) measurements cannot capture the biochemical dynamics preceding flare onset or explain the timing of severe pain manifestation. Here, we present a skin-attachable interstitial fluid (ISF)-based electrochemical sensing platform for time-resolved, minimally invasive UA monitoring in a controlled, induced mouse model of gout flare-associated inflammation and pain. The platform integrates an enzyme-based UA sensor, a thin insertion electrode, and battery-free near-field communication (NFC), enabling time-resolved in vivo tracking of ISF UA dynamics. By establishing disease-stage-specific models comprising HUA, MSU-only inflammation, and gouty arthritis flare (GA flare) conditions, we separately examined metabolic and inflammatory contributions to flare-associated UA dynamics. Time-resolved ISF monitoring revealed that the GA flare group exhibited pronounced UA fluctuation patterns that were not reproduced by either condition alone. The peak timing of UA dynamics was temporally decoupled from pain-related behavioral responses, indicating that flare-associated pain onset cannot be explained by a single UA concentration. A machine learning framework using ISF UA time-series features identified predictive information preceding peak pain, whereas analyses using earlier events defined by sustained decreases in paw withdrawal threshold showed lower and event-definition-dependent performance. These findings establish time-resolved ISF UA monitoring as a framework for resolving flare-associated biochemical dynamics and evaluating subsequent pain progression in an induced mouse model.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Wearable interstitial fluid sensing of time-resolved uric acid for early prediction of flare-associated pain in an induced mouse model

abstract: Sleep restriction leads to impaired cognitive processing across domains. I examined whether the transition to daylight saving time (DST), typically accompanied by compromised sleep, would lead to an increase in the probability of falling prey to a simulated phishing attack using a fully naturalistic experiment with random assignment and blinding. A predatory email was sent to employees at the University of California, Irvine (N = 11,218) either on the morning of Monday following the transition to DST or one week earlier. The transition led to a ~13% increase in the probability of clicking a suspicious link, without affecting the probability of opening the email or reporting it as spam. These results demonstrate that even modest, mundane, and acute loss of sleep has real-life, potentially hazardous, implications for cognitive function.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Modest loss of sleep increases susceptibility to cybersecurity threats

abstract: The translocase of the outer membrane (TOM) mediates the import of most mitochondrial preproteins. In the protozoan parasite Trypanosoma brucei , this machinery is replaced by the atypical translocase of the outer membrane (ATOM), whose composition differs substantially from the canonical TOM complexes of fungi and metazoans. Here, we report the cryoelectron microscopy structure of the T. brucei ATOM complex at 2.8 Å resolution. The structure resolves all previously identified components together with an additional, previously uncharacterized subunit. Despite its divergent composition, ATOM retains a conserved dimeric channel architecture and a protein-conducting pathway closely resembling those of opisthokont TOM complexes, indicating that the core mechanism of mitochondrial protein translocation was established early in eukaryotic evolution. In contrast, the receptor and intermembrane-space regions exhibit distinct architectures, revealing extensive evolutionary diversification and multiple examples of convergent evolution. Together, these findings provide a near-atomic view of the ATOM translocase and offer insights into the origin, conservation, and diversification of the mitochondrial protein import machinery across eukaryotes.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Structural insights into the evolution of mitochondrial protein import from the trypanosome ATOM complex

abstract: In diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL), a malignancy derived from germinal center (GC) B cells, somatic hypermutation aberrantly targets glucocorticoid receptor (GR) binding sequences in the super-enhancer (SE) of multiple oncogenes. These events abrogate GR binding and deregulate the expression of the SE-linked gene, suggesting an important role of GR in normal and transformed GC B cells. Using a GC-specific Nr3c1 knockout mouse model and multi-omics analyses in murine and human GC B cells, here we show that, under physiological conditions, GR constitutively localizes to the nucleus, where it transcriptionally modulates signaling pathways implicated in GC homeostasis and plasmablast differentiation in part by antagonizing the repressive function of BCL6 on the plasma cell master regulators IRF4 and PRDM1. While loss of baseline GR activity led to mild GC hyperplasia and impaired plasmacytic differentiation, pharmacologic doses of glucocorticoids, a key component of DLBCL chemo-immunotherapy, were preferentially toxic to GC in a GC B cell–autonomous manner. These findings uncover a physiological role for GR in the GC reaction as well as in promoting plasmablast/plasma cell formation and provide insights into the specific activity of glucocorticoids in the treatment of DLBCL.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Physiologic and pharmacologic role of the glucocorticoid receptor in germinal center B cells and plasmacytic differentiation

abstract: Theory predicts that strong species interactions drive instability in large ecosystems, but strong interactions are common in nature while strong instability appears rare. This discrepancy motivates enduring interest in ecological mechanisms that limit or counteract instability. Dormancy—reversible metabolic suppression—may be one. Dormancy is a ubiquitous life history trait found in organisms ranging from bacteria to trees. Dormant individuals form “seed banks” that are temporarily disengaged from demographic processes and species interactions, creating a memory of past ecological dynamics. Seed banks can stabilize predator–prey interactions, but whether, when, and how they affect the stability of larger ecological networks is uncertain. We show that dormancy stabilizes oscillatory dynamics in a minimal mathematical model and illustrate how dormancy converts high oscillation frequency into strong restoring force. We find that dormancy can have qualitative stabilizing effects in structured food webs that undergo Hopf bifurcations and exhibit oscillatory instability, but rarely in unstructured networks or networks with symmetric (competitive or mutualistic) interactions. This classification remains accurate when only some species go dormant and drive stabilization. Our results clarify when dormancy can promote stability, indicating that it may be an important but overlooked stabilizing factor in food webs.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Dormancy stabilizes structured food webs

abstract: Cells sense chemical gradients by absorbing ligand molecules, a nonequilibrium process that necessarily produces entropy. But how many molecules must a cell absorb, and therefore energy dissipate, to approach the physical limits of sensing? We derive closed-form expressions relating gradient sensing uncertainty to the number of absorbed molecules, which we link to entropy production. Unlike concentration sensing, which depends only on the total count, gradient sensing must resolve the angular asymmetry of the absorbed flux, adding a bounded dipole-contrast factor set by how strongly the cell absorbs. In the strong-signal regime, cells approach peak chemotactic alignment while absorbing a small fraction of the diffusion-limited uptake, with the required number of uptake events set by the relative concentration change across the cell. Re-analysis of Dictyostelium chemotaxis places the cell at 0.25% of that limit with a minor metabolic load, suggesting that sensing is limited by counting noise rather than by energetic cost.
title: Energetic costs of reaching the physical limits of sensing

abstract: Relaxation in interacting many-body systems is typically assumed to follow energy minimization, yet local dynamical rules can determine which microscopic pathways are accessible. In facilitated relaxation, these pathways are enabled or blocked by neighboring configurations. However, isolating such rules in natural materials is difficult because energetics, disorder and dynamics are usually entangled. Here we realize a geometrically tunable square-kagome artificial spin ice-a lithographic nanomagnet array-that provides a clean, designable platform for facilitated relaxation. The array hosts two tunable nearest-neighbor interactions and supports multiple low-energy phases: spin crystal, spin liquid and spin foam. In the spin-foam phase, abundant facilitator configurations allow relaxation to follow Boltzmann statistics. In the spin-crystal phase, by contrast, domain-wall excitations are trapped in non-Boltzmann distributions, although energetically preferred relaxation channels exist. The ordered crystal background lacks the facilitators needed to connect topologically distinct domain-wall classes. These classes are therefore kinetically isolated, as observed in both experiment and Monte Carlo simulation. Our results show that transition-network topology can override energetic relaxation, establishing artificial spin ice as a programmable platform for constrained dynamics and nonergodic relaxation.
title: Facilitated relaxation overrides energetic pathways in a multiphase square-kagome artificial spin ice

abstract: Absorption improves concentration sensing for an isolated cell by suppressing rebinding correlations. We study how that local advantage competes with collective depletion in assemblies of cells coupled through the shared diffusion field. We introduce an observer--absorber model for permeant ligands sensed and consumed intracellularly with finite volumetric uptake rate $κ$ that continuously interpolates between Berg--Purcell monitoring and perfect absorption. For a single spherical cell, monitoring correlations, uptake statistics and optimal joint estimator are obtained analytically, and we characterize the transition between using observer and absorber information for sensing. In this case, all sensing strategies improve monotonically with $κ$. For arbitrary cell assemblies, we show that the long-time sensing problem can be reduced to solving for just two steady-state quantities for each cell: the mean internal concentration $\Cbar$ and its local sensitivity $\Tbar=-\partial_κ\log\Cbar$. In multicellular systems, uptake shortens rebinding memory, but it also depletes the signal available to neighbors. We reveal geometry-dependent optima for absorption rates, with Pareto fronts arising from competing objectives, as well as pure observing, pure absorbing, and partially absorbing regimes.
title: Limits of cell sensing in observer-absorber assemblies
